name: Developmentalism
summary: Developmentalism holds that less developed countries escape poverty through state-led industrialisation behind tariffs, a strong internal market and deliberate planning of investment, rather than by relying on free trade and spontaneous market forces. Its Latin American form, built on Raul Prebisch and ECLA's centre-periphery analysis, supported import substitution; its East Asian form, the developmental state, used an insulated technocratic bureaucracy to guide private firms toward export industries. Both stress national autonomy and economic performance, while differing on democracy and labour.

sources.author: Raúl Prebisch
sources.usedFor: The key figure's founding text: industrialisation, protection, planning and foreign capital in Latin American development.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fonseca says the papelistas, precursors of developmentalism, rejected the "sound finance" principle of a balanced budget and admitted credit and public deficit as indispensable to lever the economy, a point that became marked in twentieth-century developmentalism (pp. 13-15).

class-collaboration.rationale: Bresser-Pereira reports that Brazilian political scientists and economists of the 1950s defined developmentalism as ideas sustaining a coalition of social classes for national development.

delink-world-market.rationale: Nassif says critics wrongly take ECLA to favour closed, inward models: its recommendations include selective and moderate protection and support for manufactured exports, with regional integration while engaging in multilateralism (section IV, pp. 12-13 and 17-18).

free-trade.rationale: The centre-periphery model contradicts the free-trade theory of comparative advantage (Nassif, section II, pp. 3-6), and Prebisch calls the old international division of labour an outdated schema whose premise was proved false by facts (1950, ch. I).

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Fonseca finds the industrial-advocacy writers tied industry to the country's independence and wanted Brazil to break its colonial position as a purely agrarian country (pp. 10-11); Jaguaribe called economic development and the consolidation of nationality two sides of one emancipatory process (Bresser-Pereira, p. 2-3).

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Industrialisation is a defining part of the developmentalist "núcleo duro", and Fonseca says that without development the nation remains in backwardness (2004, pp. 2-5; Fonseca and Salomão 2017, pp. 3-4).

limit-growth.rationale: Pro-growth intervention is part of the developmentalist core (Fonseca and Salomão, pp. 3-4), and Nassif notes that later ECLA work sought to reconcile growth with environmental limits rather than cap it (section IV).

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Fonseca and Salomão say developmentalism does not oppose the market but holds that it alone would not bring development, or only far too slowly (pp. 3-4); Bresser-Pereira says classical developmentalism held that the market could not fix prices correctly.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Fonseca defines developmentalism as a phenomenon of the capitalist world that does not attack private property, and sets it apart from planned-economy socialism (pp. 3-4).

night-watchman-state.rationale: Fonseca and Salomão's core of developmentalism is pro-growth state intervention, from planning to state firms and development banks (Fonseca 2004, pp. 1-3; 2017, pp. 3-4), the opposite of a state limited to protecting from violence.

public-ownership.rationale: Prebisch held that state enterprise should be limited to strategic necessity (Nassif, section III(a)), and Fonseca says developmentalism does not attack private property as a precondition, unlike socialism (pp. 3-4).

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Nassif reports Prebisch's view that agreements with rich countries should include exception clauses that keep open the possibility of accelerating industrial development (section III, pp. 12-13).

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Prebisch held that peripheral development must be led by national investment, with foreign capital secondary (Nassif, section III(b)), and his 1950 study calls foreign capital a temporary help to be replaced in time by domestic savings (ch. on savings, pp. 36-37).

state-directs-investment.rationale: Fonseca's hard core of developmentalism is pro-growth state intervention, from planning to state-owned firms and development banks (pp. 1-3), and Prebisch asked the State for an overall programme of investment, with state enterprise limited to strategic necessity (Nassif, section III(a), pp. 8-9).

state-harmful.rationale: Fonseca writes that for developmentalism development has to be built through action and planning, and that only the State, as the institution embodying bureaucratic and political rationality, can achieve it (pp. 4-5).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Infant-industry protection of the periphery's industry is a founding ECLA policy in Nassif's account (section III, pp. 7-10), applied selectively and gradually and relaxed as productivity rises; Fonseca lists industrialisation as part of the "núcleo duro" (pp. 2-3).

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Prebisch and Singer held that the gains of technical progress did not reach the periphery, whose terms of trade deteriorated, so that income was in effect transferred to the centre (Nassif, section II; Prebisch 1950, ch. I).

missingStatements.text: Developing countries should build their own manufacturing industry.
missingStatements.rationale: Industrialisation of the periphery is the aim of ECLA structuralism: Prebisch's study says the old division of labour left no place for it, and Nassif describes ECLA economists as favouring protection geared to the industrialization of the Latin American periphery.

keyFigures.role: Economist whose ECLA centre–periphery analysis founded Latin American developmentalism

evidence.quote: Los principales analistas del desarrollo nacional-dependiente fueron Raúl Prebisch, Celso Furtado, Osvaldo Sunkel, Aníbal Pinto, Hélio Jaguaribe e Ignácio Rangel, cuyos aportes fundamentales se hicieron en la década de 1950 y de 1960. Según el desarrollismo clásico, el mercado no podía asegurar una correcta fijación de precios microeconómicos

There is no question that the nationalist-developmentalist public policies implemented between 1950 and 1980 in many Latin American countries, including Brazil, were markedly influenced by the ideas of Prebisch

developmentalist scholars associated with the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America argued in favor of industrialization as a path to autonomous development (Furtado, 1961; Prebisch, 1950)

scope: Classical (nationalist) developmentalism, the project of ending underdevelopment by industrialisation led by a pro-growth state within capitalism, as the scholarship on it describes it: the Brazilian desenvolvimentismo whose "núcleo duro" is a national project, industrialisation and pro-growth intervention (s5, s6, s7, s8), and the ECLA structuralism of Prebisch, Furtado and Rangel that gave it its theory, with import substitution, planning and protection as its policies, mainly in Latin America from the 1930s to the 1970s (s9, s10, s12, s13). It does not take the positions of Bresser-Pereira's New Developmentalism (s11), which says it differs from the classical school, nor of the East Asian developmental state or the wider category of 'estado desarrollista' that includes mercantilism (s12); these are used only where a source says what the classical school itself held.
